The  '''white sapote''', scientific name '''''Casimiroa edulis''''', also called '''casimiroa''' and '''Mexican apple''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date=2009-02-06}}</ref> and known as ''cochitzapotl'' in the [[Nahuatl language]] (meaning "sleep-sapote") is a species of tropical fruiting tree in the family [[Rutaceae]], native to eastern [[Mexico]] and [[Central America]] south to [[Costa Rica]]. The genus is named for "an Otomi Indian, Casimiro Gómez, from the town of [[Cardonal]] in Hidalgo, Mexico, who fought and died in [[Mexican War of Independence|Mexico's war of independence]]."  <ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.calflora.net/southafrica/1C-F.html|title=Plant Names C-F|website=www.calflora.net}}</ref>

==Description==
Mature ''C. edulis'' trees range from {{convert|5|–|16|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall and are [[evergreen]]. The [[leaf|leaves]] are alternate, palmately compound with three to five leaflets, the leaflets 6–13 cm long and 2.5–5 cm broad with an entire margin, and the leaf petiole 10–15 cm long.

The [[fruit]] is an ovoid [[drupe]], 5–10 cm in diameter, with a thin, edible skin turning from green to yellow when ripe, and an edible pulp, which can range in flavor from bland to banana-like to peach to pear to vanilla [[Crème caramel|''flan'']].<ref>[https://www.flickr.com/photos/mangosteen/1245384530/ photo 1]</ref><ref>[https://www.flickr.com/photos/12103981@N03/1486266814/ photo 2]</ref><ref>[https://www.flickr.com/photos/starchmouse/525547571/ photo 3]</ref> The pulp can be creamy-white in green-skin varieties or a beige-yellow in yellow-skin varieties and has a smooth texture similar to ripe [[avocado]]. It contains from one to five large inedible seeds that are said to have [[narcotic]] properties.{{By whom|date=April 2024}}

== Chemical constituents ==
Studies carried out on the white sapote's seeds have identified many pharmacologically active compounds, including: ''N''-methylhistamine, ''N'',''N''-dimethylhistamine, and [[histamine]]. It also contains 2{{prime}},5,6-trimethoxyflavone, 2{{prime}}, 6',5,6,-tetramethoxyflavone ([[zapotin]]), and 5-hydroxy-2{{prime}},6,7-trimethoxyflavone (zapotinin).<ref name=Murillo>{{cite journal  |vauthors=Murillo G, Hirschelman WH, Ito A, etal |title=Zapotin, a phytochemical present in a Mexican fruit, prevents colon carcinogenesis |journal=[[Nutrition and Cancer]] |volume=57 |issue=1 |pages=28–37 |year=2007 |pmid=17516860 |doi=10.1080/01635580701268097 |s2cid=20080099 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1016/0040-4020(60)80001-4 | title = Constituents of Casimiroa edulis Llave et Lex.—VI 2{{prime}},5,6-Trimethoxyflavone, 2{{prime}},5,6,7-tetramethoxyflavone (zapotin) and 5-hydroxy-2{{prime}},6,7-trimethoxyflavone (zapotinin) | year = 1960 | last1 = Sondheimer | first1 = F | journal = Tetrahedron | volume = 9 | issue = 3–4 | pages = 139–144}}</ref>

== Health effects ==
Several  ''[[in vitro]]'' studies have shown that zapotin has potential anticarcinogenic effects against isolated [[colon cancer]] cells.<ref name=Murillo/><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Maiti A, Cuendet M, Kondratyuk T, Croy VL, Pezzuto JM, Cushman M |title=Synthesis and cancer chemopreventive activity of zapotin, a natural product from ''Casimiroa edulis'' |journal=[[Journal of Medicinal Chemistry]] |publisher=[[American Chemical Society]] |volume=50 |issue=2 |pages=350–5 |date=Jan 2007 |pmid=17228877 |pmc=2523270 |doi= 10.1021/jm060915+}}</ref>

The fruit has long been thought to produce drowsiness, as claimed by [[Francisco Hernández de Toledo]] in the 16th century,<ref>{{cite book|author=Morton, J.|year=1987|chapter=White Sapote: ''Casimiroa edulus'' Llave|pages=191–196|title=Fruits of warm climates|author2=Julia F. Morton |location=Miami, Florida.|url=https://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/white_sapote.html}}</ref> but this may be a misinterpretation of the [[Nahuatl]] name of the plant, ''cochitzapotl'' (meaning '"sleep-sapote"), as its seeds were processed to produce a poison by the Aztecs, and the seeds and leaves, but not fruit pulp of the plant, contain sleep-inducing compounds.{{citation needed|date=March 2025}}

==Taxonomy==

Unlike the [[mamey sapote]], white sapote is a member of the family [[Rutaceae]], to which [[citrus]] belongs.<ref>{{cite book|last=Boning|first=Charles R.|title=Florida's Best Fruiting Plants: Native and Exotic Trees, Shrubs, and Vines|year=2006|publisher=Pineapple Press, Inc.|location=Sarasota, Florida|page=211|isbn=1561643726}}</ref>
